                    ### Question
                    A 58-year-old obese male has noticed the gradual development of a soft bulge on his right groin that has been present over the past year and occasionally becomes very tender. He notices that it comes out when he coughs and strains during bowel movements. He is able to push the bulge back in without issue. After examination, you realize that he has an inguinal hernia and recommend open repair with mesh placement. After surgery, the patient returns to clinic and complains of numbness and tingling in the upper part of the scrotum and base of the penis. What nerve was most likely injured during the procedure?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Inguinal hernia repair is associated with the risk of nerve injury due to the proximity of several nerves in the groin area. The symptoms of numbness and tingling in the upper part of the scrotum and base of the penis suggest involvement of the genitofemoral nerve, which provides sensory innervation to this region. The reasoning chains consistently point to the genitofemoral nerve as the likely affected nerve, supported by the consensus that this nerve is responsible for sensation in the scrotum. Other options, such as the iliohypogastric nerve, ilioinguinal nerve, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, and obturator nerve, do not correlate with the specific symptoms presented. Therefore, the most likely nerve injured during the procedure is the genitofemoral nerve.
